claim: The hippocampal CA1 field integrates a wide variety of subcortical and cortical inputs.
source: The hippocampal CA1 field integrates a wide variety of subcortical and cortical inputs, but its synaptic organization in humans is still unknown due to the difficulties involved studying the human brain via electron microscope techniques.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation.

claim: 24,752 synapses were fully reconstructed in CA1.

claim: Most synapses in CA1 targeted dendritic spines.

claim: The hippocampus plays a crucial role in spatial orientation, learning and memory.

source: Considering both AS and SS against the four types of synaptic shapes in each layer, we found that horseshoe-shaped synapses were significantly more abundant in the SS population than in the AS population in all layers (χ2, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the synaptic shape analysis.

claim: The mean SAS area of AS was 89,727.65 nm2.
source: The mean SAS areas of AS and SS were 89,727.65 nm2 and 67,236.17 nm2, respectively
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: The mean SAS area of SS was 67,236.17 nm2.
source: The mean SAS areas of AS and SS were 89,727.65 nm2 and 67,236.17 nm2, respectively
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: The mean SAS perimeter of AS was 1,458.82 nm.
source: while the mean SAS perimeters of AS and SS were 1,458.82 and 1,378.38 nm, respectively (Table 1; Supplementary file 1L).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: The mean SAS perimeter of SS was 1,378.38 nm.
source: while the mean SAS perimeters of AS and SS were 1,458.82 and 1,378.38 nm, respectively (Table 1; Supplementary file 1L).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: No differences were observed between layers regarding the size (area and perimeter) of AS.
source: No differences were observed between layers regarding the size (area and perimeter) of the synapses both for AS (ANOVA, p>0.05; Figure 6a; Supplementary file 1L)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the synaptic size analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: No differences were observed between layers regarding the size (area and perimeter) of SS.
source: and SS (ANOVA, p>0.05; Figure 6a; Supplementary file 1L).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the synaptic size analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: AS had significantly larger areas than SS when considering all synapses together.
source: However, AS had significantly larger areas than SS when considering all synapses together (MW, p=0.032; Figure 6a; Supplementary file 1L)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the synaptic size analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: The difference in area between AS and SS was only observed in dSP, sSP and SLM when focusing on particular layers.
source: but when focusing on particular layers, this difference in area between AS and SS was only observed in dSP, sSP and SLM (MW, p=0.016, p=0.032 and p=0.008, respectively; Figure 6a; Supplementary file 1L).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the synaptic size analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: There was a strong correlation between SAS area and perimeter (R2 = 0.81 for all synapses).
source: Although significant differences in SAS area did not extrapolate to differences in SAS perimeter, there was a strong correlation between these two parameters (R2 = 0.81 for all synapses; R2 = 0.82 for AS; R2 = 0.81 for SS).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing the relationship between two measured parameters.

claim: Frequency histograms of SAS areas had similar shapes for both types of synapses with a positive skewness.
source: Frequency histograms had similar shapes for both types of synapses when considering all layers and within each layer, with a positive skewness (that is, most synapses presented small SAS area values).
evidence: This is a finding from the frequency distribution analysis.

claim: The frequency distributions of AS and SS greatly overlapped.
source: Moreover, the frequency distributions of AS and SS greatly overlapped, as did the frequency distributions of SAS area between the layers (KS, p>0.001; Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the frequency distribution analysis, supported by figures.

claim: Both AS and SS can be fitted to log-normal or log-logistic probability density functions.
source: Furthermore, we found that both types of synapses (AS and SS) can be fitted to log-normal or log-logistic probability density functions.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical modeling of synaptic size distributions.

claim: The mean SAS area of axodendritic AS (117,360.02 nm2) was larger than axospinous AS (98,200.61 nm2), but not statistically significant overall.
source: Additionally, we studied synaptic size regarding the postsynaptic targets. Although both the mean SAS area and the perimeter of axodendritic AS were larger (117,360.02 nm2 and 1,686.99 nm, respectively) than axospinous AS (98,200.61 nm2 and 1,548.38 nm, respectively), these differences were not statistically significant (MW, p>0.05; Figure 6c; Supplementary file 1M).
evidence: This is a finding from the synaptic size analysis by postsynaptic target, supported by a figure.

claim: Axodendritic AS in SLM were significantly larger than axospinous AS regarding both SAS area and perimeter.
source: Only axodendritic AS in SLM were significantly larger than axospinous AS regarding both SAS area and perimeter (MW, p=0.008 for area, p=0.016 for perimeter; Figure 6c; Supplementary file 1M).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the synaptic size analysis by postsynaptic target, supported by a figure.

claim: Axodendritic SS (71,218.23 nm2) had a larger mean area than axospinous SS (49,044.59 nm2) overall.
source: Overall, axodendritic SS (71,218.23 nm2) had a larger mean area than axospinous SS (49,044.59 nm2) (Figure 6d; Supplementary file 1M)
evidence: This is a finding from the synaptic size analysis by postsynaptic target, supported by a figure.

claim: The difference in mean SAS area between axodendritic and axospinous SS was significant only in SLM.
source: but, again, this difference in the mean SAS area was significant only in SLM (MW, p=0.032; Figure 6d; Supplementary file 1M).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the synaptic size analysis by postsynaptic target, supported by a figure.

claim: Macular synapses were smaller than complex-shaped synapses for both AS and SS.
source: Macular synapses were smaller than the rest of the more complex-shaped synapses for both AS (mean macular SAS area: 70,322.92 nm2, mean complex-shaped SAS area: 200,539.32 nm2) and SS (mean macular SAS area: 56,769.81 nm2, mean complex-shaped SAS area: 115,170.07 nm2).
evidence: This is a finding from the synaptic size analysis by shape.

claim: The difference in size between macular and complex-shaped synapses was only significant for AS.
source: However, these differences were only significant in the case of AS, as demonstrated by both mean SAS area and perimeter (ANOVA, p<0.0001 in all cases, except for macular AS and horseshoe-shaped AS, p=0.002; Figure 6e,f; Supplementary file 1N).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the synaptic size analysis by shape, supported by figures.

claim: Curvature measurements showed very little association with area (R2 = 0.05 for all synapses).
source: While synaptic size parameters area and perimeter were highly correlated (R2 = 0.81 for all synapses; R2 = 0.82 for AS; R2 = 0.81 for SS), curvature measurements showed very little association with either area (R2 = 0.05 for all synapses; R2 = 0.05 for AS; R2 = 0.00 for SS)
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing the relationship between measured parameters.

claim: Curvature measurements showed very little association with perimeter (R2 = 0.08 for all synapses).
source: or perimeter (R2 = 0.08 for all synapses; R2 = 0.09 for AS; R2 = 0.00 for SS).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing the relationship between measured parameters.

claim: No differences in the curvature of the synapses were observed between AS and SS.
source: No differences in the curvature of the synapses were observed between AS and SS (mean SAS curvature of AS: 0.050; mean SAS curvature of SS: 0.047; Figure 6—figure supplement 3a; Supplementary file 1L).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the curvature analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: No curvature differences were seen between the layers.
source: Likewise, no curvature differences were seen between the layers (ANOVA, p>0.05; Figure 6—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the curvature analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: The frequency histograms of SAS curvature ratios showed a positive skewness with a greater proportion of synapses presenting lower values.
source: The frequency histograms of SAS curvature ratios showed a positive skewness with a greater proportion of synapses presenting lower values, meaning a larger prevalence of flatter synapses than more curved ones for both AS and SS populations, but also within every layer, with great overlap among all the distributions (KS, p>0.001; Figure 6—figure supplements 1c,d and 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the frequency distribution analysis of curvature, supported by figures.

claim: The curvature ratio of axospinous and axodendritic synapses did not differ for either AS or SS.
source: Regarding the postsynaptic targets, the curvature ratio of axospinous and axodendritic synapses did not differ for either population — AS or SS (MW, p>0.05; Figure 6—figure supplement 3c,d; Supplementary file 1M).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the curvature analysis by postsynaptic target, supported by a figure.

claim: Fragmented AS were more curved than macular AS.
source: When focusing on the shape of the synaptic junction, fragmented AS were found to be more curved than macular AS (ANOVA, p=0.04) — a difference that was maintained through all layers (ANOVA, p<0.001; Figure 6—figure supplement 3e; Supplementary file 1N).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the curvature analysis by shape, supported by a figure.

claim: Fragmented SS were more curved than the rest of the synaptic shape types in SLM.
source: In the case of SS, fragmented SS were observed to be more curved than the rest of the synaptic shape types in SLM (ANOVA, p=0.0480 for macular SS-fragmented SS; p=0.0050 for HS SS-fragmented SS; and p=0.0009 for perforated SS-fragmented SS; Figure 6—figure supplement 3f; Supplementary file 1N).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the curvature analysis by shape, supported by a figure.

claim: SLM presented flatter horseshoe-shaped AS than both dSP and sSP.
source: Differences in the mean SAS curvature were also observed within the same synaptic shape type between layers. In this regard, SLM presented flatter horseshoe-shaped AS than both dSP (ANOVA, p=0.0035) and sSP (p=0.0005)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the curvature analysis by shape.

claim: SO exhibited flatter perforated AS than sSP and SR.
source: while SO exhibited flatter perforated AS than sSP (ANOVA, p=1.246×10−5) and SR (ANOVA, p=5.538×10−5; Figure 6—figure supplement 3e; Supplementary file 1N).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the curvature analysis by shape, supported by a figure.

claim: Differences between cases were observed regarding several of the parameters examined in several layers.
source: Differences between cases were observed regarding several of the parameters examined in several layers (Supplementary files 1O-AD).
evidence: This describes interindividual variability observed in the study.

claim: Differences between individual cases were not necessarily found with respect to the same parameter, or in the same layer or in the same direction.
source: Importantly, differences between individual cases were not necessarily found with respect to the same parameter, or in the same layer or in the same direction (increase or decrease).
evidence: This characterizes the nature of interindividual variability.

claim: The neuropil represents the main structural component of CA1 (more than 90% of all layers).
source: The neuropil represents the main structural component of CA1 (more than 90% of all layers).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the structural composition analysis.

claim: The contribution of SP to the total CA1 radial extension accounted for almost half of the total thickness (SP thickness: 1.13 mm; total CA1 thickness: 2.70 mm).
source: The contribution of SP to the total CA1 radial extension accounted for almost a half of the total thickness (SP thickness: 1.13 mm; total CA1 thickness: 2.70 mm).
evidence: This is a finding from the thickness measurements.

claim: Important variances can be observed in the hippocampal neuroanatomy of humans compared to rodents.
source: Indeed, important variances can be observed in the hippocampal neuroanatomy of humans compared to rodents (Amaral and Lavenex, 2007; Benavides-Piccione et al., 2020; Duvernoy, 2005; Slomianka et al., 2011; Tapia-González et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the rat hippocampus, SP is around five cell bodies thick and neuronal somata are densely packed.
source: In the rat hippocampus, SP is around five cell bodies thick and neuronal somata are densely packed, being SR the layer that contributes the most to the total CA1 thickness.
evidence: This is a comparison to rodent anatomy to contextualize the human findings.

claim: In humans, SP can be up to 30 cell somata thick, with a wider separation of neurons compared to other species.
source: In humans, SP can be up to 30 cell somata thick, with a wider separation of neurons compared to other species.
evidence: This is a finding about human CA1 anatomy.

claim: The basal and apical dendrites of human pyramidal cells are intermixed in the pyramidal cell layer.
source: As previously discussed in Benavides-Piccione et al., 2020, this sometimes refers to a 'corticalization' of the human CA1 pyramidal cell layer because it resembles a neocortical cytoarchitecture, which most probably has fundamental functional and hodological consequences: the basal and apical dendrites of human pyramidal cells are intermixed in the pyramidal cell layer (Figure 7)
evidence: This is a finding about human CA1 anatomy, supported by a citation and figure.

claim: In rodents, the basal and apical dendritic arbors are basically separated (basal dendrites in SO; apical dendrites in SR).
source: whereas in rodents, the basal and apical dendritic arbors are basically separated (basal dendrites in SO; apical dendrites in SR).
evidence: This is a comparison to rodent anatomy.

claim: Synapses were found in all layers except the alveus where they were virtually nonexistent.
source: Synapses were found in all layers except the alveus where they were virtually nonexistent.
evidence: This is a finding from the synaptic density analysis.

claim: In the mouse CA1 field, synaptic density was 2.53 synapses/µm3 in SO, 2.36 synapses/µm3 in SR and 1.72 synapses/µm3 in SLM.
source: However, in recent studies from our group using FIB/SEM to analyze the synaptic density in the rodent CA1 field, the following values were obtained: 2.53 synapses/µm3 in SO, 2.36 synapses/µm3 in SR and 1.72 synapses/µm3 in SLM in the mouse (Santuy et al., 2020)
evidence: This is data from a previous study by the authors, cited for comparison.

claim: In the rat CA1 field, synaptic density was 2.52 synapses/µm3 in SR.
source: and 2.52 synapses/µm3 in SR in the rat (Blazquez-Llorca et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from a previous study by the authors, cited for comparison.

claim: Synaptic density values in rodent CA1 are much higher than those found in human CA1.
source: These values are much higher than the ones found in the present work for the human CA1 (Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study and previous rodent studies.

claim: There are remarkable differences between the human and rodent CA1.
source: Such huge differences in synaptic density between humans and rodents —together with the above-mentioned divergences in the morphology and distribution of pyramidal cells in the SP of CA1 (Benavides-Piccione et al., 2020), as well as differences in other anatomical, genetic, molecular and physiological features (Benavides-Piccione et al., 2020; Blazquez-Llorca et al., 2020; Ding, 2013; Hawrylycz et al., 2012; Santuy et al., 2020; Tapia-González et al., 2020; van Dijk et al., 2016)— further support the notion that there are remarkable differences between the human and rodent CA1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of multiple features, supported by citations.

claim: Differences between human and rodent CA1 need to be taken into consideration when making interpretations in translational studies.
source: These differences clearly need to be taken into consideration when making interpretations in translational studies comparing one species to another.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings.

claim: Randomly distributed synapses have been described in the somatosensory cortex of rats and the frontal and transentorhinal cortices of the human brain.
source: Randomly distributed synapses have also been described in the somatosensory cortex of rats and the frontal and transentorhinal cortices of the human brain (Blazquez-Llorca et al., 2013; Domínguez-Álvaro et al., 2018; Merchán-Pérez et al., 2014; Santuy et al., 2018a)
evidence: This is a comparison to other brain regions, supported by citations.

claim: Random synaptic distribution is a widespread 'rule' of the cerebral cortex of different species.
source: suggesting that this synaptic characteristic is a widespread 'rule' of the cerebral cortex of different species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and previous literature.

claim: The neuropil is characterized by a much higher number of excitatory contacts compared to inhibitory synapses in different brain regions and species.
source: It has also been consistently reported that the neuropil is characterized by a much higher number of excitatory contacts compared to inhibitory synapses in different brain regions and species (Beaulieu and Colonnier, 1985; Bourne and Harris, 2012; DeFelipe, 2011; Domínguez-Álvaro et al., 2018; Megı́as et al., 2001; Santuy et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the mouse CA1 field, the proportion of inhibitory synapses was 8% in SLM and approximately 2% in SR and SO.
source: This data is in line with our study using FIB/SEM to analyze the synaptic density in the mouse (where the proportion of synapses that were inhibitory was 8% in the SLM, and approximately 2% in the case of the SR and SO) (Santuy et al., 2020)
evidence: This is data from a previous study by the authors, cited for comparison.

claim: In the rat CA1 field, 4% of the synapses in SR were inhibitory.
source: and in the rat CA1 field (where 4% of the synapses in SR were inhibitory) (Blazquez-Llorca et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from a previous study by the authors, cited for comparison.

claim: There is a clear preference of excitatory axons for dendritic spines and inhibitory axons for dendritic shafts in other cortical regions and species.
source: Regarding postsynaptic preferences, we observed a clear preference of excitatory axons and inhibitory axons for dendritic spines and dendritic shafts, respectively, which is also characteristic in other cortical regions and species, although variations in their percentages have been reported (Beaulieu and Colonnier, 1985; Beaulieu et al., 1992; Bourne and Harris, 2012; Domínguez-Álvaro et al., 2019; Megı́as et al., 2001; Micheva and Beaulieu, 1996; Santuy et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In layer II of the human transentorhinal cortex, axospinous AS account for only 55% of the total synaptic population.
source: For example, axospinous AS are especially abundant in sSP (87.61%) when compared to other brain regions in both humans and other species such as layer II of the human transentorhinal cortex, where axospinous AS account for only 55% of the total synaptic population (Domínguez-Álvaro et al., 2019).
evidence: This is data from a previous study, cited for comparison.

claim: Most synapses presented a simple, macular shape (86% of synapses in all layers of CA1), in agreement with previous reports in different brain areas and species.
source: Most synapses presented a simple, macular shape (accounting for 86% of the synapses in all layers of CA1), in agreement with previous reports in different brain areas and species (Domínguez-Álvaro et al., 2019; Geinisman et al., 1986; Jones and Calverley, 1991; Neuman et al., 2015; Santuy et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study compared to previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: The shape and size of the synaptic junctions are strongly correlated with release probability, synaptic strength, efficacy and plasticity.
source: The shape and size of the synaptic junctions are strongly correlated with release probability, synaptic strength, efficacy and plasticity (Biederer et al., 2017; Ganeshina et al., 2004a; Ganeshina et al., 2004b; Holderith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: All three types of non-macular synapses (with more complex shapes) were larger than macular ones.
source: In this regard, all three types of non-macular synapses (with more complex shapes) were larger than macular ones.
evidence: This is a finding from the synaptic size analysis.

claim: Perforated synapses have more AMPA and NMDA receptors than macular synapses.
source: Although the functional significance of perforations is still unclear, perforated synapses are known to have more AMPA and NMDA receptors than macular synapses and are thought to constitute a relatively powerful population of synapses with more long-lasting memory-related functionality than their smaller, macular counterparts (Ganeshina et al., 2004a; Ganeshina et al., 2004b; Vincent-Lamarre et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Perforated synapses are thought to constitute a relatively powerful population of synapses with more long-lasting memory-related functionality than macular synapses.
source: Although the functional significance of perforations is still unclear, perforated synapses are known to have more AMPA and NMDA receptors than macular synapses and are thought to constitute a relatively powerful population of synapses with more long-lasting memory-related functionality than their smaller, macular counterparts (Ganeshina et al., 2004a; Ganeshina et al., 2004b; Vincent-Lamarre et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The size of both AS and SS can be fitted to log-normal or log-logistic probability density functions.
source: The size of both types of synaptic junctions (AS and SS) can be fitted to log-normal or log-logistic probability density functions (see Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical modeling of synaptic size distributions, supported by a figure.

claim: AS and SS followed a log-normal distribution in all layers of the rat somatosensory cortex.
source: Indeed, previous studies from our laboratory found that AS and SS followed a log-normal distribution in all layers of the rat somatosensory cortex (Merchán-Pérez et al., 2014; Santuy et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is data from previous studies by the authors, cited for comparison.

claim: Some synaptic parameters such as synaptic strength and spike transmission probability follow log-normal distributions.
source: Interestingly, some other synaptic parameters —such as synaptic strength and spike transmission probability— follow log-normal distributions (for review, see Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The distribution of the size of unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSP) is very similar to the distribution of the size of SAS.
source: For example, the distribution of the size of unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSP) is very similar to the distribution of the size of SAS reported here (Lefort et al., 2009; Song et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a comparison to other synaptic parameters, supported by citations.

claim: A quantized distribution of synaptic strengths yielding a similar skewed curve was observed in the rat hippocampus when analyzing pairs of synapses formed by the same axon.
source: When analyzing the synaptic size distribution of pairs of synapses formed by the same axon, a quantized distribution of synaptic strengths yielding a similar skewed curve was observed in the rat hippocampus (Bartol et al., 2015; Bromer et al., 2018)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: It remains unclear whether a similar quantitation process occurs in the human hippocampus.
source: since we did not trace the parental axon of each segmented synapse in our samples, it remains unclear whether a similar quantitation process occurs in the human hippocampus.
evidence: This is a limitation of the current study and an open question.

claim: Activity-dependent processes seem to primarily dictate the scale rather than the shape of synaptic size distributions.
source: Although the extraordinary diversity of excitatory synapse sizes is commonly attributed to activity-dependent processes that drive synaptic growth and diminution, recent studies also point to activity-independent size fluctuations, possibly driven by innate synaptic molecule dynamics, as important generators of size diversity. Specifically, activity-dependent processes seem to primarily dictate the scale rather than the shape of synaptic size distributions (Hazan and Ziv, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Excitatory contacts were larger than inhibitory ones when considering all synapses.
source: Considering all synapses, excitatory contacts were larger than inhibitory ones, as has also been observed in layer II of the human transentorhinal cortex (Domínguez-Álvaro et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a finding from the current study compared to previous literature, supported by a citation.

claim: In the somatosensory cortex and SR of CA1 in the rat, inhibitory synapses were larger than excitatory synapses.
source: however, this contrasted with the findings in the somatosensory cortex (Santuy et al., 2018b) and SR of CA1 in the rat (Blazquez-Llorca et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Axodendritic synapses tended to be bigger than axospinous synapses, but this difference was only significant in SLM.
source: A tendency towards axodendritic synapses being bigger than axospinous synapses was also observed; however, this difference was only significant in the case of SLM synapses.
evidence: This is a finding from the synaptic size analysis by postsynaptic target.

claim: Complex-shaped AS were found more frequently associated with axodendritic AS than with axospinous AS in SLM.
source: Complex-shaped AS were also found more frequently associated with axodendritic AS than with axospinous AS in SLM, while the opposite was the case for the rest of the layers.
evidence: This is a finding from the synaptic shape analysis by postsynaptic target.

claim: In the rat hippocampus, excitatory synapses on SLM dendrites were larger than synapses in other layers.
source: These findings agree with reports in the rat hippocampus, where excitatory synapses on SLM dendrites were observed to be: (i) larger than synapses in other layers; (ii) more frequently perforated (approximately 40%); and (iii) located to a greater extent on dendritic shafts (Megı́as et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies in rats, supported by a citation.

claim: In the rat hippocampus, excitatory synapses on SLM dendrites were more frequently perforated (approximately 40%).
source: These findings agree with reports in the rat hippocampus, where excitatory synapses on SLM dendrites were observed to be: (i) larger than synapses in other layers; (ii) more frequently perforated (approximately 40%); and (iii) located to a greater extent on dendritic shafts (Megı́as et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies in rats, supported by a citation.

claim: In the rat hippocampus, excitatory synapses on SLM dendrites were located to a greater extent on dendritic shafts.
source: These findings agree with reports in the rat hippocampus, where excitatory synapses on SLM dendrites were observed to be: (i) larger than synapses in other layers; (ii) more frequently perforated (approximately 40%); and (iii) located to a greater extent on dendritic shafts (Megı́as et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies in rats, supported by a citation.

claim: The wide range of differences in the synaptic organization of the human CA1 layers may be related to the variety of inputs arriving to these layers.
source: The wide range of differences in the synaptic organization of the human CA1 layers found in the present study, especially between SLM and the rest of layers, may be related to the variety of inputs arriving to these layers (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by a figure.

claim: Detailed hippocampal human connectivity is far from being known.
source: Unfortunately, detailed hippocampal human connectivity is far to be known: data directly obtained from human brains are very scarce and most data are inferred from rodents and primates (Insausti and Amaral, 2012; Spruston and McBain, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: In the primate brain, the CA1 field receives a wide variety of inputs from multiple subcortical and cortical brain regions.
source: In the primate brain, the CA1 field receives a wide variety of inputs from multiple subcortical and cortical brain regions (Insausti and Amaral, 2012; Spruston and McBain, 2007)
evidence: This is established knowledge about primate anatomy, supported by citations.

claim: The major input to CA1 is originated in the EC.
source: being the major input to CA1 originated in the EC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CA1 connectivity.

claim: Neurons located in layer III (and layer V) of the EC project directly to SLM.
source: Specifically, neurons located in layer III (and layer V) of the EC project directly to SLM, whereas neurons in layer II project to the rest of CA1 layers indirectly via the DG and CA3 field (Insausti and Amaral, 2012; Kondo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EC-CA1 connectivity, supported by citations.

claim: Neurons in layer II of the EC project to the rest of CA1 layers indirectly via the DG and CA3 field.
source: Specifically, neurons located in layer III (and layer V) of the EC project directly to SLM, whereas neurons in layer II project to the rest of CA1 layers indirectly via the DG and CA3 field (Insausti and Amaral, 2012; Kondo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EC-CA1 connectivity, supported by citations.

claim: The synaptic organization in the layers receiving CA3 Schaffer collateral inputs (SO, SP and SR) differs from the synaptic organization found in the layer receiving direct inputs from the EC (SLM).
source: Considering both the synaptic data obtained in the present study and the connectivity knowledge in monkeys, it may seem that the synaptic organization in the layers receiving CA3 Schaffer collateral inputs (i.e. SO, SP and SR) differs with the synaptic organization found in the layer receiving direct inputs from the EC (i.e. SLM).
evidence: This is an interpretation combining the current findings with known connectivity.

claim: SLM receives a higher number of glutamatergic inputs from the amygdala and from the parietal and medial temporal cortex.
source: Additionally, SLM receives a higher number of glutamatergic inputs from the amygdala and from the parietal and medial temporal cortex and higher numbers of serotonergic and Substance-P immunoreactive fibers, with a possible extrinsic origin in the Raphe nuclei and the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus (Figure 7).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SLM connectivity, supported by a figure.

claim: SLM receives higher numbers of serotonergic and Substance-P immunoreactive fibers, with a possible extrinsic origin in the Raphe nuclei and the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus.
source: Additionally, SLM receives a higher number of glutamatergic inputs from the amygdala and from the parietal and medial temporal cortex and higher numbers of serotonergic and Substance-P immunoreactive fibers, with a possible extrinsic origin in the Raphe nuclei and the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus (Figure 7).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SLM connectivity, supported by a figure.

claim: The CA3-CA1 synaptic connection plays a key role in the learning-induced synaptic potentiation of the hippocampus.
source: It has been proposed that the CA3-CA1 synaptic connection plays a key role in the learning-induced synaptic potentiation of the hippocampus (Whitlock et al., 2006)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The direct projection from EC to SLM of CA1 seems to modulate information flow through the hippocampus.
source: while the direct projection from EC to SLM of CA1 seems to modulate information flow through the hippocampus (Dvorak-Carbone and Schuman, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: High-frequency stimulation in SLM evokes an inhibition sufficiently strong to prevent CA1 pyramidal cells from spiking in response to Schaffer collaterals input.
source: It has been reported that a high-frequency stimulation in SLM evokes an inhibition sufficiently strong to prevent CA1 pyramidal cells from spiking in response to Schaffer collaterals input (Dvorak-Carbone and Schuman, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The elevated inhibitory synapse ratio in SLM could support the finding that high-frequency stimulation in SLM evokes strong inhibition.
source: This finding could be supported by our present data showing an elevated inhibitory synapse ratio in comparison to other CA1 layers.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current findings to previous functional studies.

claim: Afferents from the EC contact not only the apical tuft of CA1 pyramidal cells, but also interneurons of the SLM.
